entities.name: Temple of Dakka
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Dakka (also: Temple of Thoth at Dakka), a Ptolemaic and Roman-era temple originally located at ancient Pselchis (Dakka) in Nubia — also saved from submersion by the Aswan High Dam's Lake Nasser through the UNESCO Nubia Campaign — is now reassembled at Wadi es-Sebua in southern Egypt, where it stands alongside the relocated temples of Wadi es-Sebua and Maharraqa as a cluster of rescued Nubian temples. The Temple of Dakka was primarily dedicated to Thoth (the god of wisdom, writing, and the moon) in his local Nubian manifestation.

Dakka's temple has an unusually complex construction history spanning several centuries: it was originally begun by the Meroitic Nubian King Arkamani (or Ergamenes I, circa 220 BCE) — making it unusual as a temple in Nubia built by the Nubian Meroitic kingdom rather than Egypt. It was subsequently expanded by Ptolemy IV Philopator (approximately 221-205 BCE) and further modified during the Roman period (Augustus through Diocletian, circa 30 BCE-300 CE). This multi-century, multi-cultural construction makes Dakka a unique example of how Nubian, Ptolemaic Greek, and Roman religious traditions interacted and overlapped at the southern margins of Egypt.

The temple's relocation and reassembly at Wadi es-Sebua makes it part of the remarkable open-air museum of relocated Nubian temples in southern Egypt — alongside Abu Simbel (moved 1968), Philae (moved 1980), Kalabsha, and others. Dakka's Thoth dedication and Meroitic origin provide valuable evidence for religious exchange between Egypt and the Nubian Meroitic Kingdom.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Dakka — uniquely begun by a Meroitic Nubian king, expanded by Ptolemies and Romans, relocated by the UNESCO Nubia Campaign, and preserved as part of the Wadi es-Sebua open-air museum — is a historically significant example of Nubian-Egyptian-Greco-Roman religious cultural synthesis.
